Straitness
strate'nes
n. (narrowness, the pressing confinement of a siege; the covenant-curse word for a people shut up until they eat their own children)
From strait — Latin strictus, drawn tight, through Old French estreit — with -ness. Not related to straight. The Hebrew is matsoq or matsor, from tsur, to confine or besiege.

Biblical Definition

Straitness means narrowness — the condition of being pressed in with no room — and Scripture uses it chiefly of a besieged city. It appears in the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 with a horror the modern reader is tempted to skip: “And thou shalt eat the fruit of thine own body, the flesh of thy sons and of thy daughters, which the LORD thy God hath given thee, in the siege, and in the straitness, wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee” (Deuteronomy 28:53), and again in verse 55. Jeremiah announces the same thing as imminent (Jeremiah 19:9), and 2 Kings 6 records it happening in Samaria. This is not rhetoric; it is what starvation inside walls did to ancient cities, and Moses set it down eight centuries before Jerusalem experienced it. Against all that stands Elihu's picture of deliverance, which uses the word to describe what God removes: “Even so would he have removed thee out of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness; and that which should be set on thy table should be full of fatness” (Job 36:16). The movement from strait to broad place is one of Scripture's standing figures for salvation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines straitness as narrowness, strictness, distress, difficulty, or want — and cites the scriptural use of a besieged people.

expand to see more

STRAITNESS, n. Narrowness; as the straitness of a place.

2. Strictness; rigor; as the straitness of a man's proceedings.

3. Distress; difficulty; pressure from necessity of any kind, particularly from poverty.

STRAIT, a. Narrow; close; not broad.

Strait is the gate and narrow is the way that leadeth to life. Matt. 7.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 28:53 — "And thou shalt eat the fruit of thine own body, the flesh of thy sons and of thy daughters, which the LORD thy God hath given thee, in the siege, and in the straitness, wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee:"

Deuteronomy 28:55 — "So that he will not give to any of them of the flesh of his children whom he shall eat: because he hath nothing left him in the siege, and in the straitness, wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee in all thy gates."

Jeremiah 19:9 — "And I will cause them to eat the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters, and they shall eat every one the flesh of his friend in the siege and straitness, wherewith their enemies, and they that seek their lives, shall straiten them."

Job 36:16 — "Even so would he have removed thee out of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness; and that which should be set on thy table should be full of fatness."

Modern Corruption

Deuteronomy 28 is dismissed as barbaric or written after the fact, which removes both the warning and the evidence of predictive prophecy.

expand to see more

Two moves are commonly made against these verses. The first is moral: a God who threatens such things is judged unworthy of worship, and the passage is set aside as belonging to a cruder stage of religion. The second is critical: the specificity of the curses is taken as proof that Deuteronomy was composed after the events it describes, during or after the exile, and dressed as prophecy. The dictionary rejects both. Mosaic authorship is the position of our Lord and the apostles, and the accuracy of the warning is exactly what a covenant document is for — the curses were published so that the people would know what they were choosing. Moses says as much in the same chapter: these things come because thou hearkenedst not unto the voice of the LORD thy God.

The moral objection deserves a plainer answer than it usually gets. Deuteronomy 28 does not describe God feeding children to their parents; it describes what happens to a walled city under siege when the covenant protection is withdrawn, and the withdrawal is announced centuries in advance with the express purpose of preventing it. The whole apparatus of prophetic warning — the repeated sendings, the rising early and sending, the long delay of judgment — is mercy operating in the open. Job 36:16 shows the direction God prefers: out of the strait into a broad place, with a table full of fatness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew matsoq, straitness or distress — Deuteronomy 28:53; matsor, a siege — the companion word; tsur, to bind or besiege; merchab, a broad place — Job 36:16.

expand to see more

Hebrew matsoq — straitness, anguish, the pressure of confinement; Deuteronomy 28:53 and 55.

Hebrew matsor — a siege, an entrenchment; joined to matsoq in the curse formula.

Hebrew tsur — to confine, to besiege; the root of both nouns.

Hebrew merchab — a broad place; Job 36:16 and Psalm 18:19, the opposite of straitness.

Latin strictus, drawn tight — the root of English strait, unrelated to straight.

Usage

"“In the siege, and in the straitness” — the covenant curse stated plainly, centuries early."

"“Out of the strait into a broad place” — the standing figure for deliverance."

"“Strait is the gate” — the same root, of the narrow way to life."
